Surf Life Saving NSW — Beach safety

blocks.text: If you're planning to spend 26 January at Bondi, here's the short version from someone who's done it more times than I can count: come early, don't bring alcohol onto the sand, swim between the flags, and treat the day thoughtfully. The beach has long been a magnet on this public holiday — historically drawing well over 100,000 people on a hot one — so a little planning turns a chaotic day into a genuinely lovely one.

Let me be honest about the tone first. 26 January means very different things to different people, and Bondi reflects that. The day used to be the most raucous of the year here — I still remember the giant inflatable Havaiana thongs and free mangoes handed out along the promenade. Those staged festivities have faded, and venues rarely advertise "Australia Day" events anymore. What's left is a big, mostly relaxed, jovial crowd enjoying the sand. That's exactly why I put this guide together: with no official programme to follow, you're on your own to plan a good day out.
Getting there and claiming your spot

Parking is at its absolute worst on this day — I genuinely wouldn't drive if I could avoid it. If you must, arrive early and settle in for the whole day rather than hoping to nip in and out. Better still, take public transport: check Transport for NSW for current bus and train options to Bondi Junction, then connect down to the beach. Fewer cars, less stress, and no circling Campbell Parade for an hour.

The good news is that even with enormous crowds, you can almost always find sand. Families do best up at North Bondi, near the shallower water and the playground. If you're kid-free, I'd drift a little further south for a quieter patch. Turn up late and the middle of the beach is usually your easiest bet.

Pack for a full day: reef-safe sunscreen, plenty of water, a hat and shade. Shops and cafés get slammed and queues are long, so bringing your own means you're not surrendering your spot to go hunting for a cold drink.

Bondi, Bronte and Tamarama are alcohol-free zones, and that's enforced hard on 26 January. Rangers and police are out in force managing crowds and traffic, and they're quick to issue on-the-spot fines for drinking on the beach and for littering. Leave the booze at home — if you want a drink, head to a licensed venue instead. Police are also on high alert given the tensions around the day, so keep it good-natured; antisocial behaviour gets very little tolerance.

blocks.title: Swim safety is non-negotiable
blocks.text: 26 January is one of the toughest days of the year for our lifesavers: huge crowds, many visitors unfamiliar with surf, and sometimes messy conditions. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags. If you can't swim confidently, stay no deeper than your knees. Caught in a rip? Stay calm, float on your back, raise an arm for help, and let the lifesavers come to you. Never swim after drinking.
Eating, drinking and a change of scene

Since nobody's running official festivities, atmosphere is where you find it. The pubs and clubs around Bondi — the likes of the Beach Road Hotel, the Royal Hotel and the local RSLs — traditionally have a good buzz, and the Bondi Pavilion precinct is a fine spot to eat with the sand right there. They all fill up fast as the day goes on, so time your run and check each venue's website or socials for opening hours and any bookings.

Want to escape the crush entirely? Bronte Beach next door is a lower-key alternative with grassy headland and a gentler crowd. Further afield in the eastern suburbs, the Clovelly Hotel and The Sheaf in Double Bay have long been popular on the day — again, check ahead before you commit.

If you'd like to mark the day more thoughtfully, Waverley Council has for several years held a community Dawn Reflection on the beach at sunrise on 26 January — a quiet gathering to acknowledge the resilience and continuing connection to Country of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, usually with a Welcome from a Traditional Custodian and a smoking ceremony. Timing and details vary year to year, so check the Waverley Council events page closer to the date for the confirmed start time and meeting point.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol on Bondi Beach on Australia Day?
items.a: No. Bondi is a designated alcohol-free zone all year round, and it's enforced strictly on 26 January with on-the-spot fines. If you want a drink, head to a licensed pub, club or bar nearby instead of bringing it onto the sand.

items.q: How early should I arrive at Bondi on 26 January?
items.a: As early as you can — mid-morning at the latest for a good spot, earlier if you're driving. Parking is at its worst all year on this day, so public transport is far less stressful. Even late arrivals can usually find room in the middle of the beach.

items.q: Is there an official Australia Day event at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Not the staged festivities of years past. The main organised gathering is Waverley Council's community Dawn Reflection at sunrise; otherwise the day is an informal, relaxed beach crowd. Check the Waverley Council events page for anything confirmed for the current year.

items.q: Where's the best place to sit with kids?
items.a: North Bondi, near the shallower water and the playground at the northern end. If you're without children, drift a little further south for a quieter stretch of sand.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi on Australia Day?
items.a: It can be, if you're sensible. Always swim between the flags where lifesavers are watching, don't go past your knees if you can't swim confidently, and never swim after drinking. Crowds and surf make it a demanding day, so respect the conditions.

blocks.text: Handled with a bit of care, 26 January at Bondi is still one of the great free days out in Sydney — golden sand, a happy crowd and that unbeatable stretch of ocean. Come early, look after each other in the water, and enjoy it.
